questions.question: In a patient presenting with progressive proximal muscle weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase (CK), what specific histological features on muscle biopsy distinguish Immune-Mediated Necrotising Myopathy (IMNM) from polymyositis or dermatomyositis?
How does the clinical timeline and response to drug cessation differentiate direct toxic rhabdomyolysis (as seen in some GLP-1 agonist cases) from drug-induced Immune-Mediated Necrotising Myopathy?

Given that approximately one-third of patients with IMNM are seronegative for anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP antibodies, how should a clinician proceed with diagnosis and management when the myositis antibody panel is negative but clinical and histological suspicion remains high?

Why might transaminases (AST and ALT) remain elevated in a patient with IMNM even after CK levels begin to normalize, and how can one determine if the source is hepatic versus muscular in a patient with known fatty liver disease?

Unlike idiopathic IMNM which often requires prolonged maintenance immunosuppression, why did this patient with suspected semaglutide-associated IMNM achieve sustained remission after a relatively short course of corticosteroids and a single cycle of IVIG?

This patient presented with dysphagia and dysphonia in addition to limb weakness. What is the significance of bulbar involvement in the context of necrotising myopathies, and does its presence alter the urgency of initiating immunomodulatory therapy?

The patient had an isolated low-titer positive anti-SS-B antibody with a negative ANA and anti-SS-A. Does this finding support a diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome-associated myositis, or is it likely an incidental finding in the context of drug-induced IMNM?

Considering the World Health Organization (WHO) Uppsala Monitoring Centre criteria for causality assessment, which three elements in this case support a 'probable' rather than 'possible' link between semaglutide exposure and the development of IMNM?
